questions.stem:
Let $\Sigma = \{a, b, c, d\}$ and let $L = \{a^i b^j c^k d^{\ell} \mid i, j, k, \ell \ge 0\}$.

Which of the following constraints ensure(s) that the language $L$ is context-free?

solutionDiagram.alt: Counter trace for constraint A, crossing arcs for constraint B and nested arcs for constraint C

steps.title: What context-free means, and the one test
steps.body: A language is context-free when some pushdown automaton accepts it: a finite control plus one stack. A stack is last-in, first-out memory, so it holds one running total at a time (its height), and it can compare two blocks only when the blocks are matched like brackets, the last symbol pushed being the first one checked. The deciding rule: join every pair of positions that the constraint forces to be equal in count. Nested joins, or a single running total, fit one stack. Joins that cross each other need two independent counters, and the pumping lemma shows such a language is not context-free. In this question the letters always come in the order $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$, so only the shape of the constraint matters.

steps.title: Option D: one total, push then pop
steps.body: $i + j = k + \ell$ says the number of $a$'s and $b$'s together equals the number of $c$'s and $d$'s together. Push one mark for every $a$ and every $b$, pop one mark for every $c$ and every $d$, and accept when the input ends with the stack empty. The stack never has to go below empty, because all pushes come before all pops. This is a deterministic PDA, so D is context-free.

steps.title: Option A: one signed total
steps.body: $i + k = j + \ell$ means $(i - j) + (k - \ell) = 0$. Keep one running total: $+1$ for each $a$ and each $c$, $-1$ for each $b$ and each $d$. The total can pass through zero and become negative, for example after $b$'s. A stack can still hold it: store the size of the total as marks on the stack, and remember the sign (plus or minus) in the finite control, which has room for one bit. A symbol that agrees with the sign pushes a mark, a symbol that disagrees pops one, and at zero the sign flips. Accept when the input ends with total zero. So A is context-free.

steps.title: Option C: nested pairs
steps.body: $i = \ell$ and $j = k$ gives $a^i b^j c^j d^i$. Pair the $b$'s with the $c$'s, and the $a$'s with the $d$'s. The $b$-$c$ pairs sit inside the $a$-$d$ pairs, so the joins nest. Push the $a$'s, push the $b$'s, let each $c$ pop a $b$, then let each $d$ pop an $a$. This is the same stack discipline as $a^n b^n$ twice, one inside the other. C is context-free.

steps.title: Option B: crossing pairs
steps.body: $i = k$ and $j = \ell$ gives $a^i b^j c^i d^j$. The $a$'s pair with the $c$'s and the $b$'s pair with the $d$'s, and the $a$-$c$ joins cross the $b$-$d$ joins. Pumping lemma with pumping length $p$: take $z = a^p b^p c^p d^p$. A window $vxy$ of length at most $p$ touches at most two neighbouring blocks, so pumping changes the counts of at most two letters and leaves the other pair unchanged, and the equalities $i = k$, $j = \ell$ break. A script that tries every window for $p = 2$ to $6$ found no window that survives. B is not context-free.

steps.title: Result
steps.body: Options A, C and D keep the language context-free; B does not. The answer is A, C and D.

shortcut.body: Write the letters in order $a\,b\,c\,d$ and draw an arc for every equality. C: $a$-$d$ and $b$-$c$ nest, accept. B: $a$-$c$ and $b$-$d$ cross, reject. A and D are sums, not pairings, so draw one counter instead: D never goes negative, and A just needs a sign bit. Unsafe step: a sum constraint that looks like crossing arcs (A) is fine, but two separate equalities that cross (B) are not. About two minutes.

traps.text: Rejecting (A) because $a$ and $c$ sit on one side of the equation and $b$ and $d$ on the other, so the arcs seem to cross. A sum equation is one total, not two pairings, and one total fits a stack with the sign kept in the finite control.
Choosing (B) because it looks like the mirror of (C). Swapping which letters pair makes the arcs cross instead of nest, and crossing pairs need two counters.
Rejecting (D) because four letters are involved. Four letters are fine when the test is a single total: push on $a$ and $b$, pop on $c$ and $d$.

recognize.clues: Each option is a condition on the exponents of $a^i b^j c^k d^{\ell}$ and the question asks whether the language is context-free, so each condition has to be turned into a picture of which counts are tied together.
recognize.contrast: Do not start by pumping every option. The pumping lemma can only show that a language is not context-free, so first try to build a stack machine, and keep pumping for the option whose links cross.

check.body: Test the crossing option by pumping $z = a^2 b^2 c^2 d^2$. Any window of length at most 2 touches at most two neighbouring blocks, so pumping it changes the count of at most two letters; for example repeating $bc$ gives $a^2 b^3 c^3 d^2$, where $i = 2$ but $k = 3$. Every other window breaks one of the two equalities in the same way. For a sum option, run the counter on a short string such as $b\,c$ ($i = 0, j = 1, k = 1, \ell = 0$ in $i + k = j + \ell$): the total goes to $-1$ and back to $0$.

variation.stem: Let $L = \{a^i b^j c^k d^{\ell} \mid i, j, k, \ell \ge 0\}$ over $\{a, b, c, d\}$. Which of the following constraints ensure(s) that $L$ is context-free?
variation.explanation: In $i = j + k$ push one mark per $a$ and pop one per $b$ or $c$; in $j + k = \ell$ push for $b$ and $c$ and pop for $d$; in $i = j$ and $k = \ell$ two matches sit side by side, one after the other. In $i = k$ and $j = \ell$ the $a$-$c$ links cross the $b$-$d$ links, so two counters are needed and the language is not context-free.

questions.stem:
Consider the following grammar where $S$ is the start symbol, and $a$ and $b$ are terminal symbols.

$S \to aSbS \mid bS \mid \epsilon$

Which of the following statements is/are true?
options: The string $abb$ has two distinct derivations in this grammar
The string $abab$ has only one rightmost derivation
The language generated by the grammar is undecidable

solutionDiagram.alt: Two different parse trees for the string abb in the grammar S → aSbS | bS | ε

steps.title: Terms: derivation, parse tree, ambiguity
steps.body: A derivation rewrites $S$ step by step, replacing one non-terminal with the right side of a rule until only terminals remain. A leftmost derivation always rewrites the leftmost non-terminal, a rightmost derivation the rightmost one. A parse tree records which rule was used at each node. Every parse tree has exactly one leftmost and one rightmost derivation, so the number of parse trees, of leftmost derivations and of rightmost derivations of a string is the same number. The rule: a grammar is ambiguous when some string has two or more parse trees.

steps.title: Count the trees for abb
steps.body: Rule $S \to aSbS$ writes an $a$, then a string $S_1$, then a $b$, then a string $S_2$, so $abb = a\,[S_1]\,b\,[S_2]$. The $b$ of the rule can be the first or the second $b$ of the string, which gives two splits. Tree 1: $S_1 = \epsilon$ and $S_2 = b$ (from $S \to bS$, then $S \to \epsilon$). Tree 2: $S_1 = b$ and $S_2 = \epsilon$. Both give $abb$, so $abb$ has two parse trees, hence two leftmost derivations and two rightmost derivations. Statements A and B are true.

steps.title: Count the trees for abab
steps.body: Again $abab = a\,[S_1]\,b\,[S_2]$, and the rule's $b$ is either the second letter or the fourth. If it is the second letter, $S_1 = \epsilon$ and $S_2 = ab$, which has exactly one tree ($a\,\epsilon\,b\,\epsilon$). If it is the fourth, $S_1 = ba$ would have to be derived from $S$; a string starting with $b$ must use $S \to bS$, which leaves the single letter $a$, and $a$ alone cannot be derived. So there is one tree, and one rightmost derivation. C is true.

steps.title: Decidability
steps.body: The language of any context-free grammar is decidable, because the CYK algorithm decides membership of a string in time $O(n^3)$. Ambiguity does not change this. D is false.

steps.title: Result
steps.body: A, B and C are true. The answer is A, B and C.

shortcut.body: Ambiguity needs only one string with two trees, and $abb$ is the quick one: the inner $b$ can come from $S_1$ or from $S_2$. That settles A and B together in under a minute. For C, try to find a second split of $abab$; there is none. D is false for every CFG, so it can be ruled out at once.

traps.text: Rejecting (C) because the grammar is ambiguous. Ambiguity is a property of some strings. A string like $abab$ can still have a single parse tree, and so a single rightmost derivation.
Marking (D) true because ambiguous grammars feel unreliable. Every context-free language is decidable, whether the grammar is ambiguous or not.

Counting derivations that differ only in the order of independent rewrites as distinct. Two derivations are different for this question only when their parse trees differ, so use leftmost or rightmost derivations to count.

recognize.clues: The grammar has a rule with an $S$ on each side of a $b$, and the statements talk about distinct derivations of one string, which is how ambiguity is defined. A count of rightmost derivations is a count of parse trees.
recognize.contrast: The last statement is about decidability, a property of the language, while ambiguity is a property of the grammar. A language can be generated by an ambiguous grammar and still be decidable.

check.body: Count the leftmost derivations by brute force: always expand the leftmost $S$ and drop any form whose terminal prefix disagrees with the target. For $abb$, the form $aSbS$ gives two survivors, $aSbS \Rightarrow abS \Rightarrow abbS \Rightarrow abb$ and $aSbS \Rightarrow abSbS \Rightarrow abbS \Rightarrow abb$. For $abab$, the form $abS$ survives only through $S \to aSbS$ then two $\epsilon$ steps; the branch through $abSbS$ needs an $a$ next and then carries two more $b$'s than the target has. So $abb$ has 2 derivations and $abab$ has 1.

questions.stem:
Consider the following context-free grammar $G$.

$S \to abaABAbba$

$A \to aaBBAb \mid bBabaa$

$B \to aBb \mid ab$

In the above grammar, $S$ is the start symbol, $a$ and $b$ are terminal symbols, and $A$ and $B$ are non-terminal symbols.

Let $L(G)$ be the language generated by the grammar $G$. For a string $s \in L(G)$, let $n_1(s)$ be the number of $a$'s in $s$ and $n_2(s)$ be the number of $b$'s in $s$.

Which of the following statements is/are true?
options: There is a string $s \in L(G)$ such that $n_1(s) < n_2(s)$
There is a string $s \in L(G)$ such that $n_1(s) > 2 n_2(s)$

solutionDiagram.alt: Table of the five productions with the a-minus-b and 2b-minus-a counts of their own terminals

steps.title: Count letters per non-terminal
steps.body: Every string a non-terminal produces has some number of $a$'s and some number of $b$'s. The surplus of a string is its number of $a$'s minus its number of $b$'s. Each rule contributes the terminals written in it plus the strings of the non-terminals it contains, so the surplus of a rule is the sum of its own terminals' surplus and the surpluses of its non-terminals. The deciding rule: find the possible surplus and the possible ratio of $a$'s to $b$'s for $B$, then $A$, then $S$, working from the inside out.

steps.title: B is balanced
steps.body: $B \to ab$ gives one $a$ and one $b$. $B \to aBb$ adds one $a$ and one $b$ around a string of $B$. So every string of $B$ is $a^k b^k$ with $k \ge 1$, with surplus $0$ and equal counts.

steps.title: A always has a positive surplus
steps.body: $A \to bBabaa$ has terminals $b, a, b, a, a$: three $a$'s and two $b$'s, plus a balanced $B$. Surplus $+1$. $A \to aaBBAb$ has terminals $a,a,b$: surplus $+1$, plus two balanced $B$'s, plus another $A$. So its surplus is $1 + \text{surplus}(A) $. The recursion can only end through $bBabaa$, so by induction every string of $A$ has surplus at least $1$. For the ratio, $bBabaa$ gives $3 + k$ against $2 + k$ and $aaBBAb$ gives $2 + m$ against $1 + m$ where $m \ge 2$ is the combined size $k_1 + k_2$ of the two $B$ blocks, so $n_1 \le 2n_2$ holds by induction for $A$.

steps.title: S combines everything
steps.body: $S \to abaABAbba$ has terminals $a,b,a,b,b,a$: three $a$'s and three $b$'s, surplus $0$. It contains a balanced $B$ and two strings of $A$, each of surplus at least $1$. So every string of $L(G)$ has $n_1 - n_2 \ge 2$. In particular $n_1 \ge n_2$ always, and $n_1 < n_2$ never happens. For the ratio, three $a$'s against three $b$'s plus pieces that each satisfy $a \le 2b$ gives $n_1 \le 2n_2$ always. The smallest string, with both $A$'s as $bBabaa$ and $B = ab$, has $n_1 = 12$ and $n_2 = 10$. Enumerating every derivation to depth four (196 distinct count pairs) gave a smallest surplus of $2$ and a largest ratio $n_1/n_2$ of about $1.29$.
steps.tex: n_1(s) - n_2(s) \ge 2 \quad\text{and}\quad n_1(s) \le 2\,n_2(s)\quad\text{for all } s \in L(G)

steps.title: Match the options
steps.body: (A) is false: no string has fewer $a$'s than $b$'s. (B) is true. (C) is false: the ratio never exceeds $2$. (D) is true. The answer is B and D.

shortcut.body: Do not enumerate strings. Spot that $B$ is balanced, so it adds nothing to either difference, then read the terminals of the other rules: $bBabaa$ has $3a, 2b$, $aaBBAb$ has $2a, 1b$ and $S$ has $3a, 3b$. Every rule has at least as many $a$'s as $b$'s and never more than twice as many, so B and D hold and A and C fail. This is safe because the bounds are checked on the terminals of each rule, not on a few sample strings.

traps.text: Choosing (A) because $B \to aBb$ and the $b$'s at the end of $S$ look like extra $b$'s. Counting the terminals of every rule shows each rule has at least as many $a$'s as $b$'s.
Choosing (C) after noticing the $aa$ at the start of $aaBBAb$. That rule has $2a$ but also $1b$ and two balanced $B$'s, so the ratio never reaches $2$.
Testing only the shortest string and concluding "for every" from it. A universal statement needs the rule-by-rule bounds, because recursion through $A$ makes infinitely many strings.

recognize.clues: The statements compare letter counts over all strings of a grammar, so the work is to read what strings each non-terminal derives, from the bottom up, rather than to list the language.
recognize.contrast: Do not reach for the pumping lemma or a stack machine. The grammar is already given, and a count that holds for each non-terminal settles every statement.

check.body: Push the ratio to its extreme. Nest $A \to aaBBAb$ many times with every $B = ab$: each level adds $4$ $a$'s and $3$ $b$'s, so the ratio of the whole string tends to $4/3$, well below $2$, while the surplus grows by one per level and never falls below its minimum.

questions.stem: Which ONE of the following languages is accepted by a deterministic pushdown automaton?
options: Any language accepted by a non-deterministic pushdown automaton.

solutionDiagram.alt: Nested language classes: regular inside deterministic context-free inside context-free inside decidable, with an example of each

steps.title: Terms: DPDA, NPDA, and the language classes
steps.body: A pushdown automaton (PDA) is a finite control with one stack. It is deterministic (DPDA) when, in every situation of state, input symbol and stack top, at most one move is possible, and an $\epsilon$-move never competes with a move that reads input. A non-deterministic PDA (NPDA) may have several choices and accepts when some choice succeeds. The languages accepted by DPDAs are the deterministic context-free languages (DCFL); NPDAs accept exactly the context-free languages (CFL). The question asks which class of languages is entirely inside DCFL, so one counter-example per wrong option is enough.

steps.title: Place the classes in a chain
steps.body: The classes sit in this order, each strictly inside the next: regular, DCFL, CFL, decidable. Strict means each step has a language that lies outside the smaller class. Option A talks about the smallest class, regular, which is inside DCFL, so every regular language has a DPDA. The other three options name classes that are bigger than DCFL.

steps.title: Why regular is inside DCFL
steps.body: Take a DFA and use it as a PDA that never touches its stack. It has exactly one move for each state and input symbol, and no $\epsilon$-moves, so it is deterministic. It accepts the same language as the DFA. A script comparing 200 random DFAs with their stack-ignoring PDAs on all strings up to length 6 found no difference. So A is correct.

steps.title: Why the others fail
steps.body: B and C are the same statement, since NPDA languages are the CFLs. The language $\{ww^R \mid w \in \{a,b\}^*\}$ is context-free but not a DCFL: a deterministic machine cannot know where the middle is. A cleaner proof uses $L = \{a^n b^n\} \cup \{a^n b^{2n}\}$: if a DPDA accepted it, one could build a PDA for $\{a^n b^n c^n\}$ from the machine, which is impossible. For D, $\{a^n b^n c^n\}$ is decidable (one left-to-right scan), but it is not context-free, so no PDA of any kind accepts it. The answer is A.

shortcut.body: Ask which option names a smaller class than DCFL. Regular is the only one: CFL and "accepted by an NPDA" are the same set, and decidable is bigger still. One counter-example kills each other option: $ww^R$ for B and C, $a^n b^n c^n$ for D. About one minute.

traps.text: Choosing (B) because "a PDA accepts it" feels the same as "a DPDA accepts it". Deterministic PDAs are strictly weaker: $ww^R$ needs a guess for the middle.
Choosing (C). Any language accepted by an NPDA is just a CFL, so this is (B) in other words and is false for the same reason.
Choosing (D) because decidable sounds like it covers everything computable. $a^n b^n c^n$ is decidable but has no PDA, deterministic or not.

recognize.clues: The question asks which whole class of languages a deterministic pushdown automaton accepts, so the clues are the word deterministic next to pushdown and options that name classes (regular, context-free, decidable) instead of single languages.
recognize.contrast: Non-deterministic pushdown automata and context-free grammars describe the same languages, so two options say the same thing. A deterministic machine is strictly weaker, and even-length palindromes mark the gap.

check.body: Use a second route through closure properties. Deterministic context-free languages are closed under complement, and the intersection of a context-free language with a regular one is context-free. Let $M = \{a^i b^j c^k \mid i \ne j \text{ or } j \ne k\}$, a union of two context-free languages. Its complement meets the regular set $a^*b^*c^*$ in $\{a^n b^n c^n\}$, which is not context-free. So if $M$ had a deterministic machine, $a^n b^n c^n$ would be context-free, a contradiction. Hence $M$ is context-free but not deterministic, and the options claiming every context-free or decidable language is deterministic all fail.

questions.stem:
Consider the two lists List I and List II given below:

For matching of items in List I with those in List II, which of the following option(s) is/are CORRECT?

solutionDiagram.alt: Closure table for context-free, recursive and regular languages under union, intersection and complement, with the verdict on each option

steps.title: What closed means
steps.body: A class of languages is closed under an operation when applying the operation to languages of the class always gives a language of the same class. Union joins two languages, intersection keeps strings in both, and complementation keeps the strings that are not in the language. One counter-example, one pair of languages in the class whose result falls outside it, is enough to show the class is not closed. A matching in an option is correct only if the property is true of the class it is paired with.

steps.title: Fill the truth table
steps.body: Context-free: union yes (join two grammars with a new start rule), intersection no ($\{a^n b^n c^m\} \cap \{a^m b^n c^n\} = \{a^n b^n c^n\}$), complement no (otherwise union and complement would give intersection). Recursive: union yes, intersection yes (run both deciders), complement yes (swap the answers), so (b) is false for it. Regular: all three yes.

steps.title: Test each option
steps.body: A pairs recursive with (b), which is false for recursive languages. D pairs regular with (b), false for regular languages. B pairs context-free with (b) (true), recursive with (a) (true), regular with (c) (true). C pairs context-free with (b), recursive with (c), regular with (a), all true. Each row of the table can have several properties true at once, which is why two options are right. The answer is B and C.

shortcut.body: Only (b) is selective: "not closed under complementation" holds for context-free languages and for neither of the other two classes. So (i) must go with (b), which kills A and D at once. In B and C the other two pairs use a property that is true of both regular and recursive languages, so both survive. About one minute.

traps.text: Choosing (A): pairing recursive languages with "not closed under complementation". Recursive languages are closed under complement because the decider's answer can be flipped; the recursively enumerable class is the one that is not closed.

Choosing (D): pairing context-free with "closed under union" is true, but regular with "not closed under complementation" is false. Swap the DFA's accept and reject states and its complement is regular.
Thinking only one option can be right. The properties in List II overlap, so the pairings are not unique; check each pairing, not just the first one that works.

recognize.clues: The question gives two lists that match language classes (context-free, recursive and regular) to closure properties, so each pair is a yes-or-no fact about an operation that keeps a language inside its class.
recognize.contrast: Closure is a different idea from decision properties such as emptiness or membership. Closure asks whether an operation stays inside the class, while a decision property asks whether an algorithm can answer a question about one language.

questions.stem:
Consider the following context-free grammar $G$, where $S$, $A$, and $B$ are the variables (non-terminals), $a$ and $b$ are the terminal symbols, $S$ is the start variable, and the rules of $G$ are described as:

$S \to aaB \mid Abb$

$A \to a \mid aA$

$B \to b \mid bB$

Which ONE of the languages $L(G)$ is accepted by $G$?

solutionDiagram.alt: Derivations in S -> aaB | Abb: the family a a b^n from aaB and the family a^n b b from Abb

steps.title: What L(G) means
steps.body: The language $L(G)$ is the set of all terminal strings that can be derived from the start symbol $S$. To find it, first find the set of strings each non-terminal derives, working from the simplest rules outward, and then substitute them into the rules of $S$. A rule such as $A \to a \mid aA$ that calls itself adds one more copy of a letter each time it is used.

steps.title: Strings of A and B
steps.body: $A \to a$ gives one $a$, and $A \to aA$ adds another $a$ in front, so $A$ derives $a^n$ for every $n \ge 1$. In the same way $B$ derives $b^n$ for every $n \ge 1$.

steps.title: Strings of S
steps.body: $S \to aaB$ gives the two fixed $a$'s followed by $b^n$, $n \ge 1$: the strings $aab, aabb, aabbb, \dots$ $S \to Abb$ gives $a^n$ with $n \ge 1$ followed by the two fixed $b$'s: $abb, aabb, aaabb, \dots$ The two families overlap in $aabb$. The two counts $n$ are free, so the number of $a$'s is not tied to the number of $b$'s. The language is the union of the families, which is option A. Enumerating all strings up to length 12 and comparing with each option confirmed that only A matches.

shortcut.body: Read the rules for what is fixed and what is free. In $aaB$ the $a$'s are fixed at two and $B$ gives any positive number of $b$'s; in $Abb$ the $b$'s are fixed at two and $A$ gives any positive number of $a$'s. Only option A has one letter fixed at two in each part. The options with $2n$ or $n$ tie the counts together, which a grammar with independent $A$ and $B$ cannot do. About 40 seconds.

traps.text: Choosing (B): reading "aa" as doubling the number of $b$'s. The $aa$ is two fixed letters, and the $b$'s come from $B$ with no link to anything else.
Choosing (C): assuming that a grammar with $a$'s on one side and $b$'s on the other produces matched counts. Matching needs a rule like $S \to aSb$; here the two parts are independent.
Choosing (D): $a^{2n}b^{2n}$ needs the counts to stay equal. Nothing in these rules compares the two counts, and $aab$ is already a member.

recognize.clues: The question gives rules and asks for $L(G)$ in closed form, so the work is to find what each non-terminal generates and substitute upwards. The options differ in which exponents are fixed and which are free.
recognize.contrast: Do not confuse this with deciding whether a language is context-free. A grammar is already given, so the language is context-free by construction and the task is only to describe it.

check.body: Test a string that separates the options: $aaabb$ comes from $S \to Abb$ with $A \Rightarrow aA \Rightarrow aaA \Rightarrow aaa$. It has three $a$'s and two $b$'s, so it lies in the family with free $a$'s and fixed $b$'s, but it is not of the form $a^n b^{2n}$, $a^{2n} b^n$, $a^n b^n$ or $a^{2n} b^{2n}$.

questions.stem:
Consider the following two languages over the alphabet $\{a, b, c\}$, where $m$ and $n$ are natural numbers.

$L_1 = \{a^m b^m c^{m+n} \mid m, n \ge 1\}$

$L_2 = \{a^m b^n c^{m+n} \mid m, n \ge 1\}$

Which ONE of the following statements is CORRECT?
options: $L_1$ is a context-free language but $L_2$ is not a context-free language.
$L_1$ is not a context-free language but $L_2$ is a context-free language.

solutionDiagram.alt: L1 needs three counts at once and fails; L2 nests its arcs, a to the last c and b to the earlier c, and a stack handles it

steps.title: The one test for a stack
steps.body: A context-free language is accepted by a finite control with one stack. A stack can check a count only by matching symbols in nested order, last pushed, first compared: think of each stack mark as a bracket that must be closed by the next letter group in reverse. So a language needs one stack when its equal counts can be drawn as nested arcs, and cannot be context-free when the arcs would need to cross or when one block must be compared with two others at the same time.

steps.title: L2 nests
steps.body: $a^m b^n c^{m+n}$ has $c^{m+n} = c^n c^m$. Write it as $a^m\,b^n\,c^n\,c^m$. The $b$'s pair with the first $n$ $c$'s, and the $a$'s pair with the last $m$ $c$'s, with the $b$-$c$ arcs inside the $a$-$c$ arcs. A stack handles this: push for every $a$, push for every $b$, pop one mark for each of the first $c$'s that matches a $b$, then pop one for each remaining $c$ that matches an $a$. A grammar is $S \to aSc \mid aXc$, $X \to bXc \mid bc$. Checked by script up to length 14, it matches the definition. So $L_2$ is context-free.

steps.title: L1 needs three counts together
steps.body: In $a^m b^m c^{m+n}$ the $a$'s and $b$'s must already be equal, and the $c$'s must outnumber that common count. A stack that has used its marks to match the $a$'s with the $b$'s has nothing left to compare with the $c$'s. Pumping lemma with length $p$, on $z = a^p b^p c^{p+1}$: a window $vxy$ has length at most $p$, so it lies in one block or in two neighbouring blocks. Pumping up inside the $a$'s or the $b$'s breaks $a = b$, or if both grow equally the $c$'s no longer exceed $m$. Pumping down inside the $c$'s leaves at most $p$ $c$'s against $m = p$. A window across the $b$-$c$ boundary loses $b$'s when pumped down. A script tried every window for $p = 2$ to $5$ and none could be pumped. So $L_1$ is not context-free.

steps.title: Result
steps.body: $L_1$ is not context-free and $L_2$ is. That is option C.

shortcut.body: Split the $c$'s of $L_2$: $a^m b^n c^n c^m$ is a nest, so it passes. In $L_1$ the $a$'s and $b$'s are already tied to each other, and the $c$'s must exceed that same number, so a third block depends on a count the stack has already spent. Three blocks tied to one number need a second counter. About two minutes.

traps.text: Choosing (A) because $L_1$ looks like $L_2$ with $n$ in a different place. In $L_1$ the $a$'s and $b$'s are already paired with each other, leaving no stack contents to compare with the $c$'s.
Choosing (B), swapping the two. Splitting $c^{m+n}$ into $c^n c^m$ is the step that makes $L_2$ nested, and a student who does not split sees three unrelated counts.
Choosing (D): $L_2$ looks hard because three letters are involved, but the stack never needs to hold three counts at once. After the $b$'s are matched to the first $c$'s, only the $a$-count remains.

recognize.clues: Two languages with exponent equations over three letters, and options asking which are context-free: each equation has to be turned into a picture of linked blocks, and the question is whether one stack can follow that picture.
recognize.contrast: The pumping lemma can show that a language is not context-free but never that it is. For a language that passes, build the stack machine or the grammar instead.

check.body: Test $L_1$ on the shortest pumpable string, $z = aabbccc$ with $p = 2$, trying each place a window of length at most 2 can sit. Inside the $a$'s, pumping up gives 3 $a$'s against 2 $b$'s. Inside the $b$'s, the same mismatch. Across the $a$-$b$ boundary, repeating $ab$ gives $aaabbbccc$, where 3 $c$'s do not exceed $m = 3$. Across the $b$-$c$ boundary, repeating $bc$ gives $aabbbcccc$, with 3 $b$'s against 2 $a$'s. Inside the $c$'s, pumping down gives $aabbcc$, where 2 $c$'s do not exceed $m = 2$. Every placement leaves $L_1$. For $L_2$, the string $abbccc$ ($m = 1$, $n = 2$) is accepted by the stack run: push $a$, push $b$, push $b$, then three $c$'s pop $b$, $b$, $a$ and leave the stack empty.

questions.stem:
Consider a context-free grammar $G$ with the following 3 rules.

$S \to aS, \quad S \to aSbS, \quad S \to c$

Let $w \in L(G)$. Let $n_a(w), n_b(w), n_c(w)$ denote the number of times $a, b, c$ occur in $w$, respectively. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?

solutionDiagram.alt: Parse tree of the string aacbc in the grammar S -> aS | aSbS | c, with the counts na=2, nb=1, nc=2

steps.title: Count what each rule adds
steps.body: Think of a derivation as a tree. Each rule changes the number of unfinished $S$ symbols and adds some terminals. Rule $S \to c$ closes one $S$ and adds one $c$. Rule $S \to aS$ keeps the number of $S$ symbols and adds one $a$. Rule $S \to aSbS$ turns one $S$ into two, so it opens one more $S$, and adds one $a$ and one $b$. A statement is true only if it holds for every $w \in L(G)$, so we need invariants that hold for all derivations.

steps.title: Find the invariants
steps.body: Start with one $S$. Each use of $S \to aSbS$ adds one extra $S$ and one $b$; each use of $S \to c$ removes one $S$ and adds one $c$. The derivation ends with zero $S$'s, so the number of $c$ rules equals one plus the number of $aSbS$ rules, and the number of $aSbS$ rules is the number of $b$'s. Hence $n_c = n_b + 1$. Each $b$ comes with an $a$ from the same rule, and some $a$'s come from $aS$, so $n_a \ge n_b$.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.body: (A) needs $n_a > n_b$, but $w = c$ has $n_a = 0 = n_b$. False. (B) $n_a \ge n_b = n_c - 1$, so $n_a > n_c - 2$. True. (C) is the invariant just proved. True. (D) needs $n_c = 2 n_b$, but $w = c$ has $n_c = 1$ and $n_b = 0$. False. An enumeration of 373 count triples from derivations up to nesting depth 5 agrees. The answer is B and C.

shortcut.body: Try the shortest string, $w = c$ with counts $(0, 0, 1)$. It breaks (A), where $0 > 0$ is false, and (D), where $1 = 0$ is false. For the survivors, notice that each $b$ is made with an extra $S$ that must end in a $c$, which gives $n_c = n_b + 1$, and then (B) follows from $n_a \ge n_b$. About two minutes.

traps.text: Choosing (A): every $b$ comes with an $a$, so $n_a \ge n_b$, but the inequality is strict only if an $aS$ rule is used. The string $c$ has no $a$ and no $b$, so $n_a > n_b$ fails.
Choosing (D): doubling looks natural because $aSbS$ has two $S$'s, but the number of $c$'s is one more than the number of $b$'s, not twice. The string $c$ has $n_c = 1$ and $n_b = 0$.
Rejecting (B) because the string $c$ has $n_a = 0$ and $n_c = 1$, and $0 > 1 - 2 = -1$ looks odd. It is true: the $-2$ leaves slack for the case $n_a = n_b$.

recognize.clues: The grammar is short and the statements relate the counts of the three terminals in every derived string, so they are invariants of derivations, found by tracking how each rule changes the number of unfinished $S$ symbols.
recognize.contrast: Do not turn this into an ambiguity question. Whether or not the grammar is ambiguous, the letter counts are the same in every parse tree of a string, so the statements are about counts, not about trees.

check.body: Substitute derived strings. The strings $c$, $ac$ and $acbc$ have $(n_a, n_b, n_c)$ equal to $(0,0,1)$, $(1,0,1)$ and $(1,1,2)$. All three satisfy $n_c = n_b + 1$ and $n_a > n_c - 2$, while $c$ already breaks the two other statements.

questions.stem: Let $G = (V, \Sigma, S, P)$ be a context-free grammar in Chomsky Normal Form with $\Sigma = \{a, b, c\}$ and $V$ containing 10 variable symbols including the start symbol $S$. The string $w = a^{30} b^{30} c^{30}$ is derivable from $S$. The number of steps (application of rules) in the derivation $S \to^{*} w$ is _________

solutionDiagram.alt: A Chomsky normal form derivation tree for a string of length 4 uses 3 binary rules and 4 terminal rules, 7 steps in all

steps.title: Chomsky normal form and what a step is
steps.body: A grammar is in Chomsky normal form (CNF) when every rule is either $A \to BC$ (two variables) or $A \to x$ (one terminal). One step of a derivation applies one rule to one variable. A derivation of a string therefore grows the sentential form in exactly two ways: a binary rule $A \to BC$ makes the form one symbol longer, and a terminal rule $A \to x$ keeps the length but turns a variable into a terminal. The deciding rule: count the two kinds of rules separately.

steps.title: Count the two kinds of step
steps.body: The string $w$ has length $n = 30 + 30 + 30 = 90$. Each of its 90 letters comes from exactly one terminal rule, so there are 90 terminal steps. The derivation starts from the single variable $S$ (length 1) and must reach 90 symbols. Only binary rules increase the length, each by 1, so there are $90 - 1 = 89$ binary steps. The count of 10 variables and the shape $a^{30}b^{30}c^{30}$ do not matter.

steps.title: Total
steps.body: $89 + 90 = 179$. A script that built 2000 random CNF derivation trees for a string of length 90 got 179 steps every time. The answer is 179.

shortcut.body: Any CNF derivation of a string of length $n$ takes exactly $2n - 1$ steps. With $n = 90$ the answer is $2 \times 90 - 1 = 179$ in ten seconds. This holds for every string of length at least 1 and every CNF grammar; it fails if the grammar is not in CNF, for example when unit rules or $\epsilon$-rules are present.

traps.text: Answering 90: counting only terminal rules and forgetting the 89 binary rules that build the tree.
Answering 89 or 180: the binary rules number $n - 1$, because starting from one variable the form grows to $n$ symbols; using $n$ gives 180, and dropping the terminals gives 89.
Using the 10 variables or the exponent 30 in the formula. The count depends only on the string length 90, not on the grammar's size or the block structure.

recognize.clues: The grammar is stated to be in Chomsky normal form and the question asks for the number of derivation steps for a string of known length, so the fixed shapes of CNF rules decide the count.
recognize.contrast: Do not reach for the CYK algorithm or the 10 variables. CYK decides whether a string is derivable, but here derivability is given and only the two rule shapes of CNF fix the step count.

check.body: Test the count on tiny strings. For a string of length 1 the only derivation is $S \to x$, one step, and for length 2 it is $S \to AB$ followed by two terminal rules, three steps. Both agree with the count of binary rules plus terminal rules, so the same bookkeeping applies at length 90.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is/are CORRECT?
options: The intersection of two regular languages is regular.
The intersection of two context-free languages is context-free.
The intersection of two recursive languages is recursive.
The intersection of two recursively enumerable languages is recursively enumerable.

solutionDiagram.alt: Closure under intersection for regular, context-free, recursive and recursively enumerable languages, with the reason for each

steps.title: What the four classes are, and what closed under intersection means
steps.body: A regular language is accepted by a finite automaton, a context-free language by a pushdown automaton (one stack), a recursive language by a Turing machine that always halts, and a recursively enumerable (RE) language by a Turing machine that accepts exactly its strings and may run forever on others. A class is closed under intersection when the strings common to two of its languages always form a language of the same class. To show closure, build a machine for the intersection from the two given machines; to refute it, give two languages in the class whose intersection is outside it.

steps.title: Regular, recursive and RE: build the machine
steps.body: Regular: run both DFAs side by side on the same input and accept when both accept (the product construction). Recursive: run the two halting machines one after the other and accept when both accept; both halt, so the combined machine halts. RE: run the first machine, and if it accepts run the second on the same input; the combination accepts exactly when both do, and it need not halt on other inputs, which RE allows. So A, C and D are correct.

steps.title: Context-free fails
steps.body: Two machines with one stack each would need two stacks to run together. A counter-example: $L_1 = \{a^n b^n c^m \mid n, m \ge 0\}$ and $L_2 = \{a^m b^n c^n \mid n, m \ge 0\}$ are both context-free, but $L_1 \cap L_2 = \{a^n b^n c^n \mid n \ge 0\}$ is not, by the pumping lemma. A script listing the strings in both languages up to length 9 returns $\epsilon$, $abc$, $aabbcc$ and $aaabbbccc$ only. So B is false. The answer is A, C and D.
steps.tex: \{a^n b^n c^m\} \cap \{a^m b^n c^n\} = \{a^n b^n c^n\}

shortcut.body: Memorise the one failure: context-free languages are not closed under intersection or complement, while regular, recursive and RE languages are closed under intersection. So pick every option except the context-free one. This is safe for intersection; it is not safe for complement, where RE fails too. About 30 seconds.

traps.text: Selecting (B): context-free languages are closed under union but not intersection. The pair $a^n b^n c^m$ and $a^m b^n c^n$ is the standard counter-example.
Leaving out (D) because RE languages are not closed under complement. Intersection is a different operation; running both machines in sequence works even though they may loop.
Leaving out (C) after confusing recursive with RE. Recursive languages are closed under intersection, union and complement.

recognize.clues: The question asks whether the intersection of two languages from the same class stays in that class, repeated across four language classes, so it is a closure-property question.
recognize.contrast: Intersection is easy to confuse with union and complement. Context-free languages are closed under union but not under intersection or complement, so check the operation named and not only the class.

check.body: Second route by De Morgan's law, $L_1 \cap L_2 = \overline{\overline{L_1} \cup \overline{L_2}}$. Regular and recursive languages are closed under complement and union, so the right side stays in the class, which agrees with A and C. Recursively enumerable languages are not closed under complement, so this route is unavailable for D and the direct run of both machines is the argument there. For context-free languages the same identity would force closure under complement, and the complement of $\{a^n b^n c^n\}$ is context-free while $\{a^n b^n c^n\}$ is not, so B fails.

Regular languages are accepted by finite automata, context-free ones by a machine with one stack, recursive ones by machines that always halt, and recursively enumerable ones by machines that may run forever on strings they do not accept.

A class is closed under intersection when two machines can be run on the same input and merged into one machine of the same power. Look at what extra memory the merged machine needs, and whether halting is preserved.
For each of the four classes, sketch the merged machine in one line. Wherever the sketch fails, look for two languages of the class whose common strings you can describe and place outside the class.

variation.stem: Which of the following classes of languages is/are closed under complement?
variation.explanation: For regular languages swap the accepting and non-accepting states of a DFA. For recursive languages run the always-halting machine and flip its verdict. Context-free languages fail because $\{a^n b^n c^n\}$ is the complement of a context-free language but is not context-free itself. Recursively enumerable languages fail because flipping the verdict does not help when the machine loops.

questions.stem:
Consider the context-free grammar $G$ below

$S \to aSb \mid X$

$X \to aX \mid Xb \mid a \mid b$,

where $S$ and $X$ are non-terminals, and $a$ and $b$ are terminal symbols. The starting non-terminal is $S$.

Which one of the following statements is CORRECT?
options: The language generated by $G$ is $(a + b)^{*}$
The language generated by $G$ is $a^{*}(a + b)b^{*}$
The language generated by $G$ is $a^{*}b^{*}(a + b)$
The language generated by $G$ is not a regular language

solutionDiagram.alt: Derivation of aabbb in S -> aSb | X, X -> aX | Xb | a | b, showing which rule produces each letter

steps.title: What the language of a grammar is
steps.body: The language of a grammar is the set of terminal strings derivable from its start symbol. A regular expression such as $a^{*}(a+b)b^{*}$ describes strings that start with any number of $a$'s, then one letter that is $a$ or $b$, then any number of $b$'s. To check a grammar against an expression, find the set derived by the inner non-terminal first and then place it inside the outer rule. A language is regular when some regular expression equals it.

steps.title: Strings of X
steps.body: $X \to a$ and $X \to b$ give the single letters. $X \to aX$ puts an $a$ on the left and $X \to Xb$ puts a $b$ on the right, in any order and any number of times. So every string of $X$ is some $a$'s on the left, one core letter, some $b$'s on the right: $a^i\,(a+b)\,b^j$.

steps.title: Wrap with S
steps.body: $S \to aSb$ adds one $a$ on the left and one $b$ on the right, $k$ times, and then $S \to X$ closes. So $L(S) = a^k\, L(X)\, b^k$. The extra $a^k$ and $b^k$ are absorbed by the stars already in $L(X)$, so nothing new is added: $L(S) = L(X) = a^{*}(a+b)b^{*}$. That is option B, which is also regular, so D is false.

steps.title: Why A and C fail
steps.body: The string $ba$ is in $(a+b)^{*}$ and in $a^{*}b^{*}(a+b)$, but $G$ cannot produce it: a $b$ is placed only as a core letter or at the right end, so nothing follows a $b$ except more $b$'s. So A and C are false. Enumerating all strings up to length 12 and comparing with each option matched only B.

shortcut.body: Test one string that separates the options: $ba$. It is in $(a+b)^{*}$ (A) and in $a^{*}b^{*}(a+b)$ (C), but no derivation puts an $a$ after a $b$. That leaves B and D, and B is regular, so D cannot also hold. Under a minute.

traps.text: Choosing (A): the rules $X \to aX \mid Xb$ look free enough to build any string, but $a$'s are only added on the left and $b$'s only on the right, so $ba$ is out.
Choosing (C): it allows an $a$ after the $b$'s, as in $aba$. The grammar puts the one free letter in the middle, followed only by $b$'s.
Choosing (D) because $S \to aSb$ looks like $a^n b^n$, which is not regular. The $a$'s and $b$'s added by $S$ are already allowed by the stars in $a^{*}(a+b)b^{*}$, so the language is regular.

recognize.clues: A small grammar is given and the question asks for the language it generates, written as regular expressions, so the work is reading what each rule adds to the strings of $X$ and then to $S$.
recognize.contrast: Do not judge regularity from the rule $S \to aSb$ alone. A rule wrapping a string in matching letters often gives a non-regular language, but here the inner part already absorbs the extra letters, so compute the set first.

check.body: List the strings of length 2 that the grammar derives. $S \to X$ gives $X \to aX \to aa$, $X \to aX \to ab$, $X \to Xb \to ab$ and $X \to Xb \to bb$, and $S \to aSb$ needs at least 3 letters. So the length-2 strings are exactly $aa$, $ab$ and $bb$. The expression $a^{*}(a+b)b^{*}$ gives the same three, while $(a+b)^{*}$ and $a^{*}b^{*}(a+b)$ both also contain $ba$.

questions.stem:
Consider the pushdown automaton (PDA) $P$ below, which runs on the input alphabet $\{a, b\}$, has stack alphabet $\{\bot, A\}$, and has three states $\{s, p, q\}$, with $s$ being the start state. A transition from state $u$ to state $v$, labelled $c/X/\gamma$, where $c$ is an input symbol or $\epsilon$, $X$ is a stack symbol, and $\gamma$ is a string of stack symbols, represents the fact that in state $u$, the PDA can read $c$ from the input, with $X$ on the top of its stack, pop $X$ from the stack, push in the string $\gamma$ on the stack, and go to state $v$. In the initial configuration, the stack has only the symbol $\bot$ in it. The PDA accepts by empty stack.

Which one of the following options correctly describes the language accepted by $P$?
questions.figure: Three states s (start), p and q. State s has two self-loops: a/⊥/A⊥ and a/A/AA. An edge from s to p is labelled b/A/ε, and p has a self-loop b/A/ε. An edge from s to q is labelled ε/A/ε and an edge from p to q is labelled ε/A/ε. State q has two self-loops: ε/A/ε and ε/⊥/ε. Here ε means nothing is read from the input or nothing is pushed.

diagram.alt: Pushdown automaton with states s, p and q: s loops on a, goes to p on b, and s, p go to q on epsilon; q pops everything

solutionDiagram.alt: Stack contents after each move of the PDA for input aaabb, accepted with an empty stack, and for aaabbb, which gets stuck in state p with only the bottom marker

steps.title: How to read the PDA
steps.body: A transition $c/X/\gamma$ means: read $c$ (or nothing, if $c$ is $\epsilon$), the top of the stack must be $X$, remove it and put the string $\gamma$ in its place. The stack starts as $\bot$. The machine accepts by empty stack: the whole input must be read and the stack must have nothing left, not even $\bot$. The rule: follow the stack. A move that needs a stack symbol that is not on top cannot be made, and a machine with no legal move simply dies without accepting.

steps.title: Phase 1: reading a
steps.body: In $s$ the stack top is $\bot$ at the start. The only move there is $a/\bot/A\bot$, so an input must start with $a$, and the empty string is rejected because the stack never empties. That move leaves $A\bot$; each further $a$ uses $a/A/AA$ and pushes one more $A$. After $a^m$, the stack holds $m$ copies of $A$ above $\bot$, with $m \ge 1$.

steps.title: Phase 2: reading b
steps.body: The move $b/A/\epsilon$ from $s$ to $p$ and the loop on $p$ each remove one $A$ for every $b$. After $b^n$ the stack has $m - n$ copies of $A$. If $n > m$ the top would be $\bot$ and no $b$ move applies, so the run dies. Once the input ends, the only way to empty the stack is to reach $q$, and the moves into $q$ both pop an $A$: $\epsilon/A/\epsilon$ from $s$ or from $p$. That needs at least one $A$ left, so $m - n \ge 1$.

steps.title: Phase 3: draining and the boundary
steps.body: In $q$ the loops $\epsilon/A/\epsilon$ and $\epsilon/\bot/\epsilon$ remove all remaining $A$'s and then $\bot$, so the stack becomes empty. For $n = m$ the stack is $\bot$ alone in state $p$. State $p$ has no move on $\bot$, and the move into $q$ needs an $A$ on top, so it is stuck with $\bot$ left and rejects. A trace of $aaabb$ ends with an empty stack, and $aaabbb$ stops in $p$ with $\bot$. So the language is $\{a^m b^n \mid m \ge 1,\ n < m\}$, option A. A search over all strings up to length 10 gave exactly this set.

shortcut.body: Count the stack. Each $a$ pushes one $A$, each $b$ pops one, and leaving for $q$ needs one more $A$ to pop, so the number of $b$'s must be strictly less than the number of $a$'s, and there must be an $a$ first. Option A is the only one with a strict $n < m$. Test the boundary $ab$: after it the stack is $\bot$ alone and the machine is stuck, so $ab$ is rejected, which rules out B. About two minutes.

traps.text: Choosing (B), allowing $n = m$, and including the empty string through $0 \le m$. With $n = m$ the stack is only $\bot$ in state $p$, and the exit to $q$ needs an $A$. The empty string has no move at all.
Choosing (C), which accepts every string of the form $a^m b^n$. The $b$'s are limited by the $A$'s on the stack: $abb$ dies on its second $b$ because $\bot$ is on top.

Choosing (D), the union of all-$a$ strings and all-$b$ strings. A string $b^n$ is rejected because the first move must be $a/\bot/A\bot$, and a string such as $aab$ is accepted although it has both letters.

recognize.clues: The machine is given as a diagram with stack operations and acceptance by empty stack, and the options differ only in the relation allowed between the counts of $a$ and $b$, so the stack height decides.
recognize.contrast: Acceptance by empty stack differs from acceptance by final state. Here a run that ends with $\bot$ still on the stack is rejected, which moves the boundary case compared with the usual $a^n b^n$ machine.

check.body: Run the boundary strings by hand. For $aab$ the stack is $A\bot$, then $AA\bot$, then $A\bot$ after the $b$, and the move into $q$ then drains it, so $aab$ is accepted. For $ab$ the stack is $\bot$ alone in state $p$, where no move applies, so it is rejected.

questions.stem:
Consider the following languages:

$L_1 = \{ww \mid w \in \{a, b\}^{*}\}$

$L_2 = \{a^n b^n c^m \mid m, n \ge 0\}$

$L_3 = \{a^m b^n c^n \mid m, n \ge 0\}$

Which of the following statements is/are FALSE?
options: $L_1$ is not context-free but $L_2$ and $L_3$ are deterministic context-free.
Neither $L_1$ nor its complement is context-free.

solutionDiagram.alt: The string aabbcc with the a-b arcs of L2 above and the b-c arcs of L3 below: the b letters are used twice, so L2 intersect L3 is a^n b^n c^n

steps.title: What each term means, and the question asks for FALSE statements
steps.body: A language is context-free if a pushdown automaton (one stack) accepts it, and deterministic context-free if a deterministic one does. A stack matches counts only in nested order. The complement of a language is every string over the alphabet that is not in it. The question asks which statements are false, so work out the truth of each statement and select the false ones.

steps.title: L2 and L3
steps.body: $L_2 = a^n b^n c^m$: push the $a$'s, pop one per $b$, then skip any number of $c$'s. The machine never has to guess where a block ends, because the letter tells it, so it is deterministic. $L_3 = a^m b^n c^n$ works the same way after skipping the $a$'s. Both are deterministic context-free. Their intersection forces $m = n$ in both, which is $\{a^n b^n c^n \mid n \ge 0\}$, and that is not context-free: the pumping lemma on $a^p b^p c^p$ finds no window that survives (checked by script for $p = 2$ to $5$).

steps.title: L1 and its complement
steps.body: $L_1 = \{ww\}$ is not context-free. Take $z = a^p b^p a^p b^p$; a window of length at most $p$ lies inside one or two neighbouring blocks, and pumping shifts the middle so the two halves no longer match (checked by script). Its complement is context-free: a string is not of the form $ww$ when its length is odd, or it is even and some letter at position $i$ differs from the letter at position $i + n/2$. A grammar is $S \to AB \mid BA \mid O$, $A \to XAX \mid a$, $B \to XBX \mid b$, $X \to a \mid b$, and $O$ generates odd-length strings. The mismatching $a$ and $b$ are separated by the same number of letters on each side. A script confirmed this grammar equals the complement up to length 12.

steps.title: Judge the four statements
steps.body: (A) $L_1$ is not context-free; $L_2$, $L_3$ are DCFL. True. (B) says $L_2$ is not context-free, but it is. False. (C) claims $L_2 \cap L_3$ is context-free, but it is $a^n b^n c^n$. False. (D) says the complement of $L_1$ is not context-free, but it is. False. The false statements are B, C and D.

shortcut.body: Check each claim against a standard fact. $a^n b^n c^m$ and $a^m b^n c^n$ are the textbook DCFLs, so A is true and B is false. Their intersection is the textbook $a^n b^n c^n$, so C is false. $ww$ is not context-free but its complement is: "false at some position" can be guessed by a PDA. That falsifies D. About two minutes.

traps.text: Selecting (A) as false after doubting that $L_2$ and $L_3$ are deterministic. The letter changes mark the block boundaries, so no guessing is needed. A is true, so it is not an answer to a question about FALSE statements.
Treating $L_2$ as non-context-free because it has three letters. Only $a^n b^n c^n$ needs three equal counts; in $L_2$ the $c$-count is free.
Thinking that the intersection of two context-free languages is context-free. Context-free languages are not closed under intersection, and $L_2 \cap L_3$ is the standard counter-example.
Assuming that if $L_1$ is not context-free then neither is its complement. CFLs are not closed under complement, so a non-CFL can have a CFL as its complement, and $ww$ is the example.

recognize.clues: Three named languages and four statements about context-freeness, determinism, intersection and complement, so each statement has to be traced to the known place of $ww$, $a^n b^n c^m$ and $a^n b^n c^n$ in the hierarchy.
recognize.contrast: The pumping lemma can show that a language is not context-free but can never show that one is. For the complement of $ww$ build a grammar or a PDA instead of trying to pump.

check.body: Test the complement of $L_1$ on strings. The string $abba$ is not of the form $ww$ because $ab \ne ba$, and the grammar derives it: $S \to AB$, $A \to a$, $B \to XBX \to XbX$, and with $X \to b$ then $X \to a$ the result is $a\,b\,b\,a$. The string $abab = (ab)(ab)$ is in $L_1$, and every string of $AB$ or $BA$ has an $a$ and a $b$ exactly half the length apart, while $abab$ has equal letters at distance 2 and no unequal pair there. Separately, $abc$ and $aabbcc$ meet the conditions of both $L_2$ and $L_3$, while $aabbc$ is in $L_2$ only.

questions.stem: Let $L_1$ be a regular language and $L_2$ be a context-free language. Which of the following languages is/are context-free?

solutionDiagram.alt: Each option simplified using L1 regular and L2 context-free: B equals L1 intersect L2, C equals all strings, D equals L2, A can leave the context-free class

steps.title: Terms and the three facts that decide it
steps.body: The complement $\overline{L}$ of a language is the set of all strings over the alphabet that are not in $L$. Three facts decide the question. Regular languages are closed under complement, union and intersection. A context-free language intersected with a regular language is context-free (run the PDA and a DFA together). Context-free languages are not closed under complement, so $\overline{L_2}$ may not be context-free. A statement is correct only if the language is context-free for every choice of $L_1$ regular and $L_2$ context-free.

steps.title: Simplify B, C and D with set algebra
steps.body: B: by De Morgan's law, $\overline{\overline{L_1} \cup \overline{L_2}} = L_1 \cap L_2$, a regular language intersected with a context-free one, so context-free. C: $L_2 \cup \overline{L_2}$ is every string, $\Sigma^{*}$, and $L_1 \cup \Sigma^{*} = \Sigma^{*}$, which is regular. D: $(L_1 \cap L_2) \cup (\overline{L_1} \cap L_2) = (L_1 \cup \overline{L_1}) \cap L_2 = \Sigma^{*} \cap L_2 = L_2$, which is context-free. A script checked these identities on 300 random pairs of languages.
steps.tex: B = L_1 \cap L_2,\qquad C = \Sigma^{*},\qquad D = L_2

steps.title: A can fail
steps.body: Take $L_1 = \Sigma^{*}$, which is regular, and $L_2 = \overline{\{a^n b^n c^n\}}$, which is context-free: a string is outside $a^n b^n c^n$ when its letters are out of order or the three counts are not all equal, and a PDA can guess which. Then $L_1 \cap \overline{L_2} = \overline{\overline{\{a^n b^n c^n\}}} = \{a^n b^n c^n\}$, which is not context-free. So A is not always context-free. The answer is B, C and D.

shortcut.body: Simplify with De Morgan first. B becomes $L_1 \cap L_2$, C becomes $\Sigma^{*}$, D becomes $L_2$, all context-free. Only A leaves a complement of $L_2$ standing, and that is the one that breaks. Any option where $\overline{L_2}$ survives is suspect. About one minute.

traps.text: Selecting (A): intersecting with a regular language preserves context-free, but the thing being intersected is $\overline{L_2}$, and context-free languages are not closed under complement.
Rejecting (B) because the expression has two complements. Apply De Morgan's law and the complements cancel: it is just $L_1 \cap L_2$.
Rejecting (C) because $L_2 \cup \overline{L_2}$ involves a complement. The union of any language and its complement is all strings, which is regular.

recognize.clues: Each option combines a regular language $L_1$ and a context-free language $L_2$ with union, intersection and complement, so the closure facts of both classes apply once each expression is simplified.
recognize.contrast: Intersection of two context-free languages is unsafe, but intersection with a regular language is safe. The trap is to treat $\overline{L_2}$ as if it were context-free.

check.body: Substitute extreme choices. With $L_1 = \Sigma^{*}$, option B becomes $\overline{\overline{L_2}} = L_2$, which matches $L_1 \cap L_2$. With $L_1 = \emptyset$, option D becomes $\emptyset \cup (\Sigma^{*} \cap L_2) = L_2$, which is context-free as claimed. With $L_1 = \emptyset$ option A is $\emptyset$, so a counterexample for A must use a different $L_1$.

questions.stem:
For a string $w$, we define $w^R$ to be the reverse of $w$. For example, if $w = 01101$ then $w^R = 10110$.

Which of the following languages is/are context-free?

solutionDiagram.alt: Mirror arcs for the four languages with w = pq and x = rs: option A has crossing arcs, B, C and D have none

steps.title: The mirror test
steps.body: A stack reads back the symbols it has stored in reverse order, which is what $w^R$ is. So a pushdown automaton can check that a second block is the reverse of a first block when the two blocks are paired like brackets, as in $ww^R$. Draw an arc between each symbol and its mirror partner. If all arcs nest, one stack handles it and the language is context-free. If arcs cross, two stacks would be needed and the language is usually not context-free. A language is context-free exactly when a pushdown automaton accepts it.

steps.title: B, C and D have no crossing arcs
steps.body: B: $ww^Rxx^R$ is an even palindrome $ww^R$ followed by another even palindrome $xx^R$. Each part is context-free, and a concatenation of two context-free languages is context-free. C: $wxw^R$ with $x$ any string is all of $\{0,1\}^{*}$, because $w = \epsilon$ is allowed and then any string is $x$. It is regular, so context-free. D: $wxx^Rw^R$ puts $x x^R$ inside $w \ldots w^R$, so the arcs nest: it is exactly $(wx)(wx)^R$, an even palindrome, with a standard PDA. A script confirmed B equals the concatenation of two palindrome sets, C equals all strings and D equals the even palindromes, all up to length 12.

steps.title: A has crossing arcs
steps.body: In $wxw^Rx^R$ the $w$ pairs with $w^R$ and $x$ pairs with $x^R$, but $x$ lies between $w$ and $w^R$ while $x^R$ lies after $w^R$. The arc for $w$ spans $x$'s start and the arc for $x$ spans $w^R$'s start, so they cross. To prove it, intersect with the regular set $0^{+}\,1\,0^{+}\,111\,0^{+}\,11\,0^{+}$. The words of A in it are exactly $0^p\,1\,0^q\,111\,0^p\,11\,0^q$ (checked for all block sizes 1 to 15), where the first and third blocks and the second and fourth blocks must match. The pumping lemma on $0^p 1 0^p 111 0^p 11 0^p$ finds no window that survives, so the intersection is not context-free, and since context-free is closed under intersection with a regular set, A is not context-free. The answer is B, C and D.

shortcut.body: Put $w$ and $x$ on a line and draw the mirror arcs. B, C and D are nested or free, so pick them. A is the only one where the second arc starts inside the first and ends outside it, so reject it. Decide in two minutes; the pumping proof is not needed in the exam.

traps.text: Selecting (A) because it uses the same pieces as the others. The order $w\,x\,w^R\,x^R$ makes the arcs cross, which needs two stacks.
Rejecting (B) after seeing two reversals. Each reversal sits next to its own copy ($ww^R$, then $xx^R$), so the arcs are side by side and a stack handles them one after another.
Rejecting (C) because it has $w$ and $w^R$ with an unrelated $x$ between them. Taking $w = \epsilon$ shows the language is all strings, so the $w^R$ constraint costs nothing.
Rejecting (D) because it has two reversed blocks. The $x\,x^R$ is nested inside $w \ldots w^R$, so it is simply the palindrome $(wx)(wx)^R$.

recognize.clues: Each option arranges $w$, $x$ and their reverses in a fixed order, and context-freeness depends on whether the pairing between a block and its reverse nests or crosses.
recognize.contrast: Reversal pairs well with a stack but plain repetition does not. A block that is allowed to be empty can also make a language collapse to all strings, which is regular.

check.body: Test each language on one short word. B: with $w = 01$ and $x = 10$, the word $0110\,1001$ is $ww^R$ followed by $xx^R$, so two side-by-side palindromes fit B. C: with $w = \epsilon$ and $x = 1101$ the word is just $x$, so any string is in C. D: with $w = 01$ and $x = 1$ the word $011110$ is an even palindrome, and any even palindrome $uu^R$ fits D with $w = \epsilon$, $x = u$. A: with $w = 0$ and $x = 1$ the word is $0\,1\,0\,1$, where the first $0$ pairs with the third symbol and the $1$ in the middle pairs with the last, so the two pairings overlap and one stack cannot follow both.

questions.stem: Suppose that $L_1$ is a regular language and $L_2$ is a context-free language. Which one of the following languages is NOT necessarily context-free?

steps.title: Terms and the rule that decides it
steps.body: A language is a set of strings. It is regular if a finite automaton accepts it, and context-free if a context-free grammar generates it (equivalently, a pushdown automaton accepts it). A class of languages is closed under an operation if applying the operation to members always gives a member. The complement $\overline{L}$ is every string over the alphabet that is not in $L$, and $L_1 - L_2$ is the set of strings in $L_1$ that are not in $L_2$. The rule: context-free languages are closed under union, concatenation, and intersection with a regular language, but not under complement and not under intersection of two context-free languages. "NOT necessarily context-free" asks for the operation that can leave the class for some regular $L_1$ and some context-free $L_2$.

steps.title: The three operations that are safe
steps.body: A, $L_1 \cap L_2$: run a finite automaton for $L_1$ and the pushdown automaton for $L_2$ side by side on the same input and accept when both accept. The pair is still one machine with one stack, so the result is context-free. B, $L_1 \cdot L_2$: a regular language is context-free, and concatenation of two context-free languages is context-free (new start rule $S \to S_1 S_2$). D, $L_1 \cup L_2$: new start rule $S \to S_1 \mid S_2$. These three are context-free for every choice, so none is the answer.

steps.title: Option C can leave the class
steps.body: $L_1 - L_2$ is $L_1 \cap \overline{L_2}$, and $\overline{L_2}$ need not be context-free. Take $L_1 = \{a,b,c\}^{*}$, which is regular, and $L_2 = \overline{\{a^n b^n c^n \mid n \ge 0\}}$. $L_2$ is context-free: a string is outside $a^n b^n c^n$ when its letters are out of order (it contains $ba$, $ca$ or $cb$) or two of the three counts differ, and a grammar can guess which. A script built that grammar and matched it with the definition on all 29,524 strings of length up to 9, of which 29,520 are in the complement. Then $L_1 - L_2 = \{a^n b^n c^n\}$, which the pumping lemma shows is not context-free. So C fails, and the answer is C.

shortcut.body: Only complement breaks context-free languages here. Rewrite each option: A, B and D never complement a context-free set, but $L_1 - L_2$ hides $\overline{L_2}$ inside it. Pick C. About 30 seconds, and safe because the other three are standard closure facts.

traps.text: Reading intersection as unsafe because two context-free languages can intersect to a non-context-free one. That is true for two context-free languages, but here one side is regular, and a regular language adds no stack, so $L_1 \cap L_2$ stays context-free.
Thinking concatenation can fail. Context-free languages are closed under concatenation, and a regular language is context-free, so $L_1 \cdot L_2$ is context-free for every choice.
Thinking union with a regular language can fail. A grammar for the union just adds one start rule, $S \to S_1 \mid S_2$, so union is always safe.

recognize.clues: The wording "NOT necessarily context-free" with one regular and one context-free language, and four standard operations including a set difference, asks which operation is not closed.
recognize.contrast: The differences $L_1 - L_2$ and $L_2 - L_1$ look alike but differ: the complement lands on a regular language in one and on a context-free language in the other, and only the second lets the result leave the class.

check.body: Second route by contradiction. Suppose $L_1 - L_2$ were context-free for every regular $L_1$ and context-free $L_2$. Taking $L_1 = \Sigma^{*}$ would make the complement of every context-free language context-free. Context-free languages are closed under union, so De Morgan's law would then give closure under intersection too. But $\{a^n b^n c^m\} \cap \{a^m b^n c^n\} = \{a^n b^n c^n\}$ is not context-free, so the supposition fails and the difference is the operation that can leave the class.

The number of strings of length 100 accepted by the above pushdown automaton is ______.

steps.title: Terms and the rule that decides it
steps.body: A pushdown automaton (PDA) is a finite automaton with a stack. A move written $a, X \to Y$ on an arrow means: read the input symbol $a$ ($\epsilon$ means read nothing), require $X$ on top of the stack and pop it ($\epsilon$ means ignore the stack), then push $Y$ ($\epsilon$ means push nothing). A string is accepted if some run of moves reads all of it and ends in a final state; here the only final state is $q_3$, and what is left on the stack does not matter. So to count accepted strings, find which input strings have a run whose every move is allowed by the stack.

steps.title: Read what each state does
steps.body: $q_0 \to q_1$ pushes the bottom marker $\#$. In $q_1$ each $a$ is read and an $A$ is pushed, so after $i$ letters $a$ the stack holds $\#$ and $i$ copies of $A$. The move $q_1 \to q_2$ is free. In $q_2$ each $b$ is read and one $A$ is popped, so $j$ letters $b$ need $j \le i$. The move $q_2 \to q_3$ with $\epsilon, A \to A$ needs an $A$ on top, so at least one $A$ must remain: $i - j \ge 1$. $q_3$ has no outgoing move, so all input must be read before it. Because $q_1$ reads only $a$ and $q_2$ reads only $b$, every accepted string has the form $a^i b^j$. A script ran this machine on every string of length up to 14 and the accepted set was exactly the strings $a^i b^j$ with $i > j$.

steps.title: Count the strings of length 100
steps.body: Length 100 means $i + j = 100$, and $i > j$ means $j < 50$. So $j$ takes the values $0, 1, \dots, 49$, and each gives one string ($a^{100}$, $a^{99}b$, $\ldots$, $a^{51}b^{49}$). The script also ran the machine on all 101 strings $a^i b^{100-i}$ and 50 were accepted. The answer is 50.

shortcut.body: Read the machine as: $a$ pushes, $b$ pops, and at the end one more $A$ must still sit on top. That is $a^i b^j$ with $i > j$. For length 100, $j$ runs from 0 to 49, so 50. About 2 minutes. It is unsafe only if you forget that the last move needs an $A$ to be present.

traps.text: Answering 51 by counting $i \ge j$, which includes $a^{50}b^{50}$. After its 50 b-moves the stack top is $\#$, the move $\epsilon, A \to A$ cannot fire, and the string is rejected.
Answering 49 by dropping $j = 0$. The string $a^{100}$ has no b-moves, leaves 100 copies of $A$, and is accepted.
Answering 101 by accepting every $a^i b^{100-i}$. That ignores that each $b$ must pop an $A$ and that an $A$ must remain for the last move.

recognize.clues: The PDA is drawn, not described: one loop pushes on $a$, a second loop pops on $b$, and a final arrow needs a symbol on top. The question then counts the accepted strings of one length, so the first job is to read off the language.
recognize.contrast: This is not a design task (pda-design), where you build a machine for a given language. Here the machine is given and you must extract its language, remembering that acceptance is by final state, so symbols may stay on the stack.

check.body: Shrink the length and count by hand. For length 4 the strings $a^ib^{4-i}$ are $bbbb$, $abbb$, $aabb$, $aaab$, $aaaa$. Only $aaab$ and $aaaa$ leave an $A$ on top for the last arrow, so 2 are accepted, which is half of 4. The count at length 100 follows the same rule, one string for each number of $b$ below half the length.

questions.stem: Consider the language $L = \{a^n \mid n \geq 0\} \cup \{a^n b^n \mid n \geq 0\}$ and the following statements. I. $L$ is deterministic context-free. II. $L$ is context-free but not deterministic context-free. III. $L$ is not LL($k$) for any $k$. Which of the above statements is/are TRUE?

solutionDiagram.alt: Deterministic pushdown automaton for a^n union a^n b^n with states A, B and F; A and F are final

steps.title: Terms and the rule that decides it
steps.body: A language is context-free if a grammar generates it. It is deterministic context-free (DCFL) if a deterministic pushdown automaton (DPDA) accepts it, meaning that in every configuration at most one move is possible, so the machine never has to guess. Every DCFL is context-free, but some context-free languages, such as even-length palindromes, are not DCFL. A grammar is LL($k$) if a top-down parser, reading the input left to right and building a leftmost derivation, can always pick the next production by looking only at the next $k$ input symbols. The rule: to show a DCFL, build a DPDA; to refute LL($k$), show that no fixed number of lookahead symbols can force the choice.

steps.title: Statement I is true, so II is false
steps.body: Build a DPDA with a bottom marker $Z$. State $A$ is final: each $a$ pushes an $a$ and stays in $A$, so every string $a^n$ is accepted. On the first $b$ the machine pops an $a$ and moves to $B$; each further $b$ pops one more $a$. When the top is $Z$ again, a free move goes to the final state $F$. So $a^n b^n$ is accepted, and $a^n b^m$ with $m \ne n$ is not: with $m < n$ an $a$ is left on top, with $m > n$ there is no move. Each configuration has at most one move, so the machine is deterministic. A script compared it with $L$ on all strings up to length 12. So $L$ is a DCFL: I is true and II is false. That already removes B (II only) and D (III only).

steps.title: Statement III is true: no lookahead tells $a^n$ from $a^n b^n$
steps.body: The natural grammar is $S \to A \mid B$, $A \to aA \mid \epsilon$, $B \to aBb \mid \epsilon$. While the parser is still reading $a$s, the input $a^n$ and the input $a^n b^n$ look identical for the next $k$ symbols whenever more than $k$ letters $a$ remain, so the parser cannot choose between $A$ and $B$. This holds for every $k$ (a script found $\mathrm{FIRST}_k(A\$)$ and $\mathrm{FIRST}_k(B\$)$ share $a^k$ for each $k$ tried). Other grammars for $L$ fail for the same reason: a top-down parser must commit, after reading only $a$s, to the stack it will use, and the two cases need different stacks (nothing left to match for $a^n$, exactly $n$ symbols $b$ to match for $a^n b^n$). The full proof for every possible grammar is longer than an exam needs and is not reproduced here; it is the textbook result that $\{a^n\} \cup \{a^n b^n\}$ is deterministic yet not LL($k$) for any $k$. Only the argument for the natural grammar above is checked here. III is true.

steps.title: Combine
steps.body: I is true, II is false, III is true. The statements that are true are I and III only, option C.

shortcut.body: I is a quick yes: push $a$s, pop on $b$s, accept at the end of the $a$s or at the empty stack. That removes II and "III only". Between "I only" and "I and III only", ask whether any fixed lookahead can tell $a^n$ from $a^n b^n$. It cannot, because they differ only after $n$ symbols. Pick I and III. About 2 minutes.

traps.text: Choosing I only: believing every deterministic language is LL($k$) for some $k$. LL($k$) is stricter than deterministic; here the decision must be made before the first $b$ appears, which can be arbitrarily far away.
Choosing II only: thinking a union of $a^n$ and $a^n b^n$ forces a guess between the two cases. The machine never needs to guess, because the $b$s reveal which case it is in.

Choosing III only: seeing that the language is not LL($k$) and concluding it is not deterministic. A DPDA can read the whole input before it decides, so being non-LL($k$) says nothing against being a DCFL.

recognize.clues: One language is a union of a plain block of $a$s and a matched $a^nb^n$, and the statements use deterministic acceptance and LL($k$) together. The branch is only revealed by the first $b$, which can be far away.
recognize.contrast: Do not read LL($k$) as a synonym for deterministic. DCFL is about acceptance by a deterministic machine, which may read to the end before deciding; LL($k$) is about predicting productions with a fixed lookahead, and is the stricter condition.

check.body: Run the machine on the short strings that separate the two parts. The strings $\epsilon$, $a$ and $ab$ are accepted and $b$ and $abb$ are not, with one move available at every step. For lookahead take $k = 3$: the strings $aaaa$ and $aaaabbbb$ share their first 3 symbols, so with the natural grammar a parser has to choose a branch before the input separates them, and a larger $k$ moves the same collision further out.

options: $L_1$ is context-free but not regular and $L_2$ is context-free.
$L_1$ is context-free but $L_2$ is not context-free.

steps.title: Terms and the rule that decides it
steps.body: A language is regular if a finite automaton accepts it, which means a regular expression describes it and no unbounded counting is needed. It is context-free if a grammar generates it. $(0+1)^+$ means one or more symbols from $\{0,1\}$, and $|x|$ is the length of $x$. Both languages say "there exist $w$, $x$, $y$ such that ...". The rule: simplify what the existence really demands. Often a long witness can be replaced by a single symbol, which turns a copy language into a plain pattern, and a "differs somewhere" condition is something a grammar can guess.

steps.title: $L_1$ is regular
steps.body: A string is in $L_1$ when it is $w\,x\,y\,x$ with $w$, $x$, $y$ nonempty. The copy $x$ can be cut down to one symbol: if $x = zc$ with last symbol $c$, then $wxyx = (wz)\,c\,(yz)\,c$, and both $wz$ and $yz$ are nonempty. So $s \in L_1$ exactly when $s = u\,c\,v\,c$ with $u$, $v$ nonempty and $c$ a single symbol. That is a regular expression. A script compared it with the definition on all binary strings up to length 12. So $L_1$ is regular, and therefore also context-free.

steps.title: $L_2$ is context-free
steps.body: A string $z = xy$ has even length $2n$, and $x \ne y$ means some position $i \le n$ holds a different letter from position $n + i$. Cut $z$ into two blocks of odd length, the first centred at position $i$ and the second centred at position $n+i$. Each block has equal stretches on both sides of its centre, and the two centres are exactly $n$ apart. Conversely, an odd block followed by an odd block with different centre letters has even total length and centres exactly half the length apart. So $L_2$ is "an odd block with centre $a$ followed by an odd block with centre $b$, or the reverse". Here $A$ makes odd strings centred on $a$, $B$ makes odd strings centred on $b$, and $X$ is any letter. A script checked this grammar against the definition on all strings up to length 12.
steps.tex: S \to AB \mid BA,\quad A \to XAX \mid a,\quad B \to XBX \mid b,\quad X \to a \mid b

steps.title: Choose the option
steps.body: $L_1$ is regular and $L_2$ is context-free: option A. Option B says $L_1$ is not regular, which is false. Option C says neither is context-free, which is false. Option D says $L_2$ is not context-free, which is false.

Option A. About 2 minutes. The shortcut is unsafe if you treat $wxyx$ like the copy language $\{ww\}$ and require the whole $x$ to be remembered.

traps.text: Choosing B: reading $wxyx$ as a copy that needs memory of $x$, so it looks non-regular. But $x$ may be one symbol, and then only the last letter matters.
Choosing C: treating both as copy languages like $\{ww\}$, which is not context-free. $L_1$ is regular and $L_2$ asks for a difference, which a grammar can find by guessing the position.
